title: Apple’s iPhone Duo Pre‑Orders: Mark Gurman Calls It a “Major Mistake” – MacRumors Report
body:
Apple’s decision to open pre‑orders for the new iPhone Duo this week has drawn sharp criticism from industry analysts, who argue the company ignored clear warning signs that the device would be hamstrung by “severe supply constraints.” The criticism was voiced most prominently by Mark Gurman, a veteran Apple reporter, who described the move as a “major mistake” that could erode consumer confidence and complicate Apple’s broader supply‑chain strategy.

The iPhone Duo, slated to launch later this month, is Apple’s first attempt at a dual‑screen smartphone, a concept that promises new multitasking capabilities but also demands a more complex manufacturing process. According to insiders, Apple was aware as early as the summer that the novel hinge mechanism and the need for two high‑resolution displays would stretch its existing production lines. Despite this, the company proceeded with a pre‑order window that began on Friday, offering the device to customers before it had secured sufficient inventory to meet demand.

Analysts point out that Apple’s pre‑order model traditionally serves as a gauge of market appetite while also building hype for a product that is ready to ship in large numbers. In the case of the Duo, the pre‑order launch appears to have been driven more by a desire to generate buzz than by logistical readiness. “Opening pre‑orders when you know you can’t fulfill them is a gamble that undermines the brand’s reputation for reliability,” Gurman said in a recent interview. “It also puts pressure on retailers who may have to turn away eager customers or issue refunds, which is a costly and brand‑damaging exercise.”

The timing of the decision is also notable given Apple’s recent supply‑chain challenges. The company has wrestled with component shortages across its product lines, from chip scarcities that have delayed Mac and iPad shipments to logistical bottlenecks that have slowed iPhone deliveries in key markets. By pushing forward with the Duo pre‑orders, Apple may be attempting to signal confidence in its ability to overcome these hurdles, but the move could backfire if the anticipated supply crunch materializes. Early reports from a handful of authorized resellers indicate that inventory is already thin, with many customers receiving messages that the device is “out of stock” shortly after placing an order.

From a strategic perspective, Apple’s gamble may be tied to its broader push into differentiated hardware. The Duo represents a potential new product category that could open revenue streams beyond the incremental upgrades of its flagship iPhone line. If the device succeeds, it could justify the engineering investment and set a precedent for future form‑factor innovations. However, the risk is that a poorly executed rollout could reinforce consumer skepticism about Apple’s ability to deliver on ambitious hardware concepts, especially as competitors like Samsung and Huawei continue to refine foldable and dual‑screen technologies.

Looking ahead, Apple will need to act quickly to mitigate the fallout from the pre‑order controversy. Strengthening communication with both customers and retail partners about realistic delivery timelines will be essential to preserve trust. Additionally, the company may need to accelerate production ramp‑up, perhaps by diversifying its supplier base or allocating additional resources to the hinge and display manufacturers. If Apple can navigate these challenges and deliver the iPhone Duo on schedule, it could still carve out a niche in the premium smartphone market. Conversely, a prolonged shortage could serve as a cautionary tale about the perils of overpromising on cutting‑edge hardware without securing the supply chain first. The coming weeks will reveal whether Apple’s bold pre‑order push will pay off or become a footnote in its storied history of product launches.
